To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the oxidation of Polish coals in the temperature range 323–523 K resulted in the generation of CO2 and CO in amounts of up to 1.5 and 0.3% volume, respectively, and the ratio of CO/CO2 increased along with temperature.
CO2 is a major oxidation product, while the amounts produced of CO and H2 were low and did not exceed 1%.
the amount of CO2 generated from coal oxidation increases with increasing temperature, while the amount of CO produced increases only up to 423 K and decreases at higher temperatures.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the determination of the oxidation products of Polish coal samples and the analysis of their relationships with the physical-chemical coal properties.
the development of an experimental methodology to assess the fire hazard of coals in mine atmosphere.
a new approach to the problem of coal self-heating and its potential hazards, which is the determination of the oxidation gases profile.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the amount of CO and H2 generated during oxidation of coals with a low ash and high carbon content is low and does not pose a risk of spontaneous ignition.
the amount of fire gases emitted from coal is dependent on its physical-chemical properties.
the higher the coal rank, the lower the amount of CO2 and H2 emissions, while the amount of CO emission was not dependent on the coal rank.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the amount of CO and CO2 produced in the coal oxidation process was related to the content of carbon and oxygen in the sample.
coal with higher inertinite content is more susceptible to spontaneous heating than the one with higher carbon content.
the amount of CO2 produced during coal oxidation was the largest and the amount of CO was the second largest.
The main takeaway from our work is that
coal with higher oxygen content and inertinite content, as well as lower carbon content, is more prone to self-heat.
the oxidation products profile is a good predictor of coal self-heating.
the emission profile is a valuable indicator of the coal self-heating hazard.
